Residents like us, meanwhile, are just trying to grow our own food (and, perhaps like us, doing so without having a green lawn at all). We homestead on our small lot of land, and our water bills are frequently over $300 throughout the summer. That is water used entirely to irrigate crops, that feed our family and and neighbors, with water-efficient drip irrigation systems. subject: Let's Do Our Part/D5
comment: Hello! I am a passionate birdwatcher here in SLC and would like to bring your attention to the Lights Out program, which can benefit birds and also save our building energy and money. Every year, billions of birds migrate north in the spring and south in the fall, often flying at night--navigating with the night sky. However, bright artificial lights and sky glow from big cities can disorient them, causing them to collide with buildings or windows. This confusion and exhaustion can lead to vulnerability to other urban threats. Dozens of species, including priority species such as the Allen's Hummingbird, Wood Thrush, and Golden-winged Warbler, are affected by this problem. Fortunately, a simple act of turning off lights can help birds navigate our environment and protect them from unnecessary harm. The Audubon's Lights Out program is a national effort to reduce this problem, and participating in this program can make a significant difference. For example, in a landmark study conducted by the Field Museum in Chicago, turning off lights in one building reduced the number of birds killed there by over 80 percent. I urge you to participate in Lights Out by turning off unnecessary lighting, putting necessary lighting on timers or using motion sensors, making sure external lighting is down shielded, and dimming or extinguishing lobby or atrium lighting, particularly between the hours of midnight and sunrise and during spring and fall migration periods (April/May and September/October). In addition to helping birds, these efforts have the additional benefits of reducing energy usage and saving money. Thank you for considering this request. If you can make these simple changes in your building or buildings, you can truly have a positive impact on the birds that share our community. For more information--Tracy Aviary is one of Audubon's local Lights Out collaborators. Sincerely, Nick Carpenter

subject: The council's acceptance of drunken driving
comment: To the Salt Lake City Council, I was deeply disturbed by the statement put out by the council regarding councilwoman Amy Fowler's recent DUI arrest. To reference police statements which she hasn't refuted, she was driving at more than twice the legal limit at 11 a.m. on a weekday, was involved in a crash, drove away (for many miles), and when police found her visibly impaired, lied to them about having used alcohol. All of this, in apparently every single council member's estimation, is nothing more than a simple "mistake" that shouldn't disqualify Councilwoman Fowler from the privilege of representing Salt Lake City and making important decisions for the city. The message is clear: this level of poor judgment is a level of judgment openly welcome on the council. The line in the public statement that "as the City Council, we consider the safety and well-being of the public our utmost priority" is nonsensical and blatantly false. If that statement were true, the council would—at the very barest minimum humanly possible—have reacted to one of its members endangering the lives of its constituents by saying something in its official statement directly against drunken driving, a serious crime that kills and maims thousands of Americans per year. Instead, the message was one of acceptance—that in Salt Lake City, getting behind the wheel while impaired is nothing more than an understandable error that happens to the best of us. Council members either don't understand how this episode has destroyed the entire council's credibility or don't care. Either option is very concerning to me as an SLC resident, and I hope if Councilwoman Fowler doesn't do the honorable thing and resign, the rest of you come to your senses about how you're reacting. Sincerely, Jade McDowell

subject: Gross Disturbance of the Peace and the Right to Safety and Security
comment: Council Member Mano and Interested Parties. We are writing to describe a neighborhood incident that occurred Saturday, May 13, 2023: At 1:00 PM on Saturday our neighbors to the west, tenants in a rental house at REDACTED South, were actively setting up for a large party. The set up included amplified music, drums, and acoustic instruments. We were never informed of this event beforehand. We preemptively contacted the landlord and told him of our objections to amplified music, drums, and apparently an open invitation to a large crowd. The landlord told us that he would contact the tenants and "find out what's going on." One of the tenants appeared in our driveway and informed us that they were proceeding with the party but would not activate the amplifiers. He also informed us that he had missed the City's permitting window for amplified music, which we doubted at the time. The tenant who talked to us was abrupt and hostile. Over the course of the next 10 hours, a rotating group of at least 50 to 75 people circulated and the party became increasingly loud, with attendees in our yard and cars periodically blocking our driveway. Other than the three residents of the house, we had no idea who any of these people were - were they hostile, armed, or intent on property damage? Amplified music, banjos, drums, and other instruments were played at such a loud volume that we were driven from our house at REDACTED South due to the deafening noise. We contacted the Salt Lake City Police Department repeatedly, described this situation, and asked for assistance because we are two elderly gay men who are defenseless against an onslaught of at least 50 thirty year olds. The police finally arrived at 10:30 PM after 5 of our phone calls asking for help, spoke to several party attendees, and left after about 5 minutes. The party resumed, at full volume for another hour and a half, as soon as the police officer drove away. These tenants obviously know that we are old gay men who would be unable to do anything about this party, a gross disturbance of our peace. Because of who we are, it seemed obvious to us that these party goers assumed we could do nothing to protest or stop the noise. They were apparently right because the police department's response was ineffective and our repeated complains were entirely ignored. Is there anything more that can be done so that situations like this do not happen in the future? Is there a viable reason the police no longer respond effectively and in a timely manner to these complaints? Does the right to have a loud, disturbing party somehow supersede the right to peace and quiet in one's own house? Is there anything that the Council Liaison and the Council can do to assure us of equal treatment as citizens of Salt Lake City? Robert Barth Hal Gonzales

subject: Council Fowler and the City Council Statements about recent Fowler's recent DUI Arrest... Not nearly enough...
comment: Mrs. Mayor and Council Members, I want to thank Councilwoman Fowler for stepping down as the RDA Board Vice Chair. That was the right thing to do and a first small step in rebuilding trust with the constituents in her district and everyone else in our city. I want to also thank the remainder of the council members for their statement regarding Councilwoman Fowlers DUI arrest. I agree that "it is important to recognize that, as humans, Council Members make mistakes and errors." and that we should all make an effort to extend "...compassion and grace to all individuals, including our Council..." members. However, I am not only very disappointed that Mayor Mendenhall has said nothing , but I am completely disheartened that no one has made any substantive statement about driving under the influence and the terrible acts that surround it. Making statements about having an "eye opening experience" that has made one reflect on their "relationship with alcohol" and being clear that "we consider the safety and well-being of the public our utmost priority" are not nearly enough, not by a long shot. Councilwoman Fowler is of course innocent until proven guilty, but it is clear to everyone after reading the numerous news articles about this incident, that there are clear and undisputed facts surrounding the allegations against her. The Councilwoman's statement referencing alcohol is a confirmation in and of itself that she acknowledges at least one of those undisputed facts. That fact would be that that she drew a breath test of 0.111, more than double our legal limit, is enough to make no direct mention by anyone that she was driving under the influence equally irresponsible as driving under the influence. To not talk about that kind of elephant in the room by any of you does nothing to rebuild trust in Councilwoman Fowler, the entire Council, or the mayor. It does a lot to make us question if Councilwoman Fowler is really owning her mistake and if the Council and mayor are taking this issue as seriously as they should by holding her accountable for her actions. If you really want to be clear about how you all feel about driving under the influence, make a statement about the real risks of the all too often horrific outcomes that come from it. A statement that Councilwoman Fowler herself and everyone else that day that came into contact with her were extremely lucky all that occurred was a minor car accident and that no one was injured or killed. Nothing any of you have said so far expresses the true serious nature of what occurred. What Councilwoman Fowler said and the statement from the Council relay to me and many others is that you are all attempting to minimize and downplay the seriousness of what happened. I am thankful nothing more than a minor car accident and her arrest where the result of the choices Councilwoman Fowler made that day. I am thankful no one was hurt, that she wasn't hurt, and that she can deal with whatever issues she has going on as it relates to alcohol or otherwise. It could have so easily had such a more terrible and disastrous outcome. But, the residents of our city heard the statements you made and they wonder if you all really think driving under the influence is a big deal or not. We wonder this because your statements relayed to us that you don't really think it's that serious. With weak statements that minimize what occurred, it feels like you are all holding yourselves to a standard everyone else knows they would not be afforded. I know it will hurt, possibly even be damaging; personally, politically, or otherwise for all of you. But surely, you can't think that minimizing this like you have so far, allegations or not, is the answer or the right thing to do. Isn't the car, or rather the elephant already out of the bag? Please don't continue to do what we have grown far too used to seeing from our elected leaders. Instead, make statements about the true serious nature of what occurred; bring it out into the open, do not leave it in the shadows. Bring the truth into the light so we can truly and sincerely rebuild the trust and you can reaffirm how serious driving under the influence really is. Right now, it feels far too familiar. It's not just a "mistake" or an "error", minimizing it isn't "compassion" or "grace". You all surely already know we expect more from you, that expectations for you are higher, you are not just another resident of the city, you are our elected leaders. Nothing so far any of you have said has made me feel like something as serious as this is anything but politics as usual, and I can't see how any true rebuilding of trust will come from it. There are many voices calling for Councilwoman Fowler, the City Council, and the mayor to minimize what happened, or in the case of the mayor, say nothing at all. Your fellow Salt Lake City resident, Casey O'Brien McDonough Lower Avenues, Salt Lake City
